summary:
“Space Mission: Beyond Limits” is a co-operative multiplayer game where players can feel like the leaders of a space mission and see how each of their actions affects the outcome of the game. The game supports teams of up to four players, and each player has their own role in managing the mission. 
The game shatters the stereotype that physics and engineering are boring subjects detached from reality. Players try their hand at being real space specialists and put their knowledge into practice – specifically, in designing and carrying out the mission. This is important, as the game helps to foster players’ interest in science, physics and engineering, whilst also teaching them to make decisions independently and work as a team.
details:
Space Mission: Beyond Limits is a cooperative, educational 3D browser game designed for 2–4 players. It allows participants to step into the roles of space agency specialists and try their hand at managing a space mission. Each player oversees a specific department and has access only to a particular portion of the mission data. Consequently, participants must interact, share information, and make decisions collectively. Every decision impacts the shared spacecraft and the ultimate outcome of the entire mission.

During the game, the team designs a spacecraft while accounting for engineering constraints such as structural mass, budget, power consumption, and thermal management. Once a design is complete, players send the craft toward Titan or an asteroid, where they may encounter technical malfunctions, loss of communication, or even equipment failures.

The game is unique in that it does not automatically correct players' mistakes as they happen. Instead, the system warns of potential risks, allowing the team to make their own decisions and take responsibility for every choice they make. Once a mission is complete, a final report is generated, showing the players the outcome of the expedition an outcome shaped by the decisions they made.

Our main advantage lies in the combination of STEM education, engineering modeling, and team-based interaction. Unlike other educational games, ours places a greater emphasis on collective responsibility, independent decision-making, and the consequences of one’s actions.

The project is relevant because it fosters the development of practical scientific knowledge, engineering thinking, and teamwork skills among adolescents and the general public.According to the results of the international OECD PISA 2025 study, an average of 74% of students in OECD countries report that they are interested in learning how various things work. This indicates a sense of curiosity that is important to support and foster through hands-on learning.Furthermore, according to the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs 2025 report, 69% of surveyed employers consider analytical thinking a key professional skill, while 61% highlight leadership and social interaction. These figures underscore the importance of the skills that our game is designed to develop.

When developing the project, our team takes into account scientific accuracy, realistic engineering constraints, gameplay accessibility, synchronization of actions among multiple players, user-friendly interface design, and educational value. We also strive to strike a balance between scientific complexity and engaging gameplay, ensuring that the experience remains accessible even to those without in-depth knowledge of physics or engineering.

Languages: TypeScript (main), JavaScript (Node.js scripts), GLSL (effect shaders), SQL, Python (build scripts), HTML/CSS.

Frameworks: React 19, three.js + React Three Fiber + drei (WebGL 3D), zustand, Web Audio API (sound synthesized in code), custom EN/RU localization.

Backend & infrastructure: Supabase (PostgreSQL + Realtime, Row Level Security) for online multiplayer, Vercel hosting, GitHub + GitHub Actions CI.

Dev & testing: Vite, pnpm, Node.js 22, Git, Vitest (269 automated tests incl. the spec’s acceptance tests A–F), Puppeteer + Chrome for device emulation, glTF-Transform + meshoptimizer for 3D models, Obsidian for docs.

AI tools: Claude Design (3D models, UI design), ChatGPT (icons, concept art), Claude (texts, translation, documentation).
dataRefs: NASA's upcoming New Frontiers mission to Titan is called Dragonfly. Because Titan possesses a dense, nitrogen-rich atmosphere and low gravity, NASA designed a dual-quadcopter (rotorcraft) to fly through the atmosphere and land at various locations to investigate prebiotic chemistry. The UI states that a "Rotor System" is a mandatory requirement, described as the primary method of transportation across Titan.

The constructor requires an "RTG" as the mandatory main energy source, while the "Solar Panel Array" is marked as useless. It also includes a "High-Capacity Battery" to store energy for peak loads. Furthermore, players must carefully route power across main and secondary lines to avoid overloadsSolar power is completely ineffective under Titan's hazy atmosphere. Dragonfly relies on an MMRTG, which converts the heat generated by the natural decay of plutonium-238 into a continuous supply of electricity (about 110 watts). Because flying requires immense power, this steady electricity trickle-charges a high-capacity battery, which then provides peak power to the rotors during flights. The excess heat from the RTG is also critical for keeping spacecraft instruments from freezing..

These objectives perfectly match the actual scientific payload of the Dragonfly rotorcraft: DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DraGNS (Gamma-ray/Neutron Spectrometer) for analyzing surface chemistry and biologically relevant compounds; DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology) for atmospheric profiles, monitoring conditions, and temperature; Camera suites for capturing terrain images and guiding the rotorcraft safely.

To transmit data back home, distant spacecraft must accurately point their High-Gain Antennas toward Earth. Because deep-space bandwidth is heavily restricted and shared among many missions via the Deep Space Network, data must be highly prioritized, compressed, and queued into packets for transmission based on the current link quality.

Titan is the only moon in our solar system with a dense atmosphere (four times denser than Earth's) and the only other world with stable liquid on its surface. This further validates the "Atmosphere Profile" and "Surface Chemistry" mission priorities, as NASA is actively studying Titan's methane cycle and complex organic chemistry.

This game mode directly mirrors NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission. In 2023, OSIRIS-REx successfully returned to Earth with a sample of rocks and dust collected from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu, providing vital data about the early solar system.

Deep space autonomous flight requires Hazard Avoidance Cameras (Hazcams), LiDAR, and Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) to navigate the hazy surface safely. Real-time remote piloting from Earth is impossible due to light-speed delays, making these autonomous modules critical.To survive the -179°C (-290°F) ambient temperature, the spacecraft hull relies on thick aerospace insulation (such as aerogel) and an active thermal loop system. This system pumps excess heat generated by the RTG directly into the core electronics module to prevent the internal computers and batteries from freezing

A Learning Game About Telescop. Much like NASA's educational telescope game, "Titan: Sky Explorer" teaches that scientific objectives dictate the engineering characteristics of a space mission. Players learn that ambitious scientific goals require complex, carefully coordinated engineering decisions and severe constraints, rather than just picking the most expensive modules.
